lesson.title: Hobbys I: die Musik, der Sport, das Lied, tanzen, malen
lesson.subtitle: what you do when the work stops — and the word German borrowed back from English

hook.title: The Muses, the Reverse Loan, and the Lost Song
hook.content: Five words for what you do when the work stops — and they arrive by four different roads. die Musik is the oldest purchase: Latin musica, from Greek mousikē, 'the art of the Muses' — the nine goddesses of song, poetry and memory. English made the same Greek purchase as music; the two are one loan in two spellings, and both keep the Muses' k at the end. der Sport traveled the opposite way: English shortened Old French desport, 'amusement', into sport, and in the nineteenth century German bought the short English form outright — sport had never been a German word before, so this is a straight purchase from English, made in the very decades English was buying Kindergarten and Angst from German. das Lied is the lost-cousin story: it is one and the same ancient word as Old English leod, 'song' — a word Germany kept and England dropped. When English speakers today say Lied for a German art song, they are using Germany's survivor for the twin they lost. tanzen came off the French shelf: French danser, the very word English took as dance — one French purchase, two buyers, and the difference between the d of dance and the t of tanzen is where and when each language bought the loan, not a sound law. And malen keeps the strangest twin of the five: it belongs to the Germanic word behind das Mal, 'mark, spot' — and that word's English twin is alive in the least expected place: the mole, the small dark mark on the skin, from Old English māl. English paints with Latin pingere, but it kept the old mark-word — it just moved it to the skin. That is the whole story — and the lesson's one word with no twin is das Lied, whose Old English partner leod England dropped.

footnotes.title: The Receipts Run Both Ways
footnotes.content: Loans are receipts for contact, and between neighbours the traffic never runs one way. German gave English Kindergarten, Angst, Zeitgeist and Doppelgänger; English gave German der Sport, das Hobby — and even der Keks, which is English cakes respelled and re-gendered by German. When a word crosses the border twice, you can watch two centuries shake hands.

pattern.title: The Hobby Frames
pattern.content: 1. The verbs are regular: ich tanze, du tanzt, er tanzt; ich male, du malst, er malt — strip the -en, add the person ending. 2. The noun frames: Musik kommt aus dem Radio (music comes from the radio), Das Lied kommt vom Klavier, Mein Hobby ist Musik. 3. The frequency adverb sits right after the verb, as in English: Ich tanze selten (I seldom dance), Wir gehen oft ins Kino. 4. The idiom the drills use: Ich tanze gern — gern, 'gladly', is German's like + -ing; with sport the fixed phrase is Ich treibe gern Sport, literally 'I drive sport gladly'. 5. Three genders on one hobby shelf — learn them with the article: die Musik, der Sport, das Lied.
pattern.linguist_note: Borrowings that run both ways are the sound of two languages at eye level. For a thousand years the heavy traffic ran Latin and French into both languages; the newer traffic — Kindergarten into English, Sport into German — only started once Germany and England were peers reading each other's newspapers. der Sport even kept the English short form, not the French desport: a borrowed word can arrive second-hand and still become the standard.

exercises.prompt: The free evening — match each hobby sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: The song comes from the piano
The singer and the farmer sing a song
matching_pairs.german: Der Sänger und der Bauer singen ein Lied

matching_pairs.english: The music from Ireland is beautiful
matching_pairs.german: Die Musik aus Irland ist schön

matching_pairs.english: The song is in my language
matching_pairs.german: Das Lied ist in meiner Sprache

matching_pairs.english: On the holiday there is sport on TV
matching_pairs.german: Am Feiertag ist Sport im Fernsehen

matching_pairs.english: The sock is in the shoe

exercises.target_answer: Musik kommt aus dem Radio, Das Lied kommt vom Klavier, Mein Hobby ist Musik, Der Sänger und der Bauer singen ein Lied, Die Musik aus Irland ist schön, Das Lied ist italienisch, Der Arzt sagt: mehr Sport!, Das Lied ist in meiner Sprache, Wir malen ein Haus, Wir tanzen zur Musik, Am Feiertag ist Sport im Fernsehen, Die Socke ist im Schuh
exercises.meaning: music, songs, sport, shoes, painting — the free evening
exercises.explanation: One free evening, in sentences. Music owns its prepositions — aus dem Radio, vom Klavier — and the old professions join in: der Sänger und der Bauer singen ein Lied. The hobbies hang on the people you already know.

exercises.prompt: One of today's five is German's straight purchase from English — a word German had never had before the nineteenth century. Which?
exercises.meaning: der Sport ← English sport ← Old French desport: German's 19th-century purchase
exercises.explanation: die Musik is a Greek loan both languages made separately; das Lied is native Germanic; tanzen is French, the same purchase as dance. der Sport is the odd one: English shortened Old French desport to sport, and German bought the short English form in the nineteenth century.

diagnosis.slip: guessing die Musik because it looks modern
diagnosis.cue: die Musik is the oldest word here — Greek via Latin; the modern-looking one is the loan from English

exercises.prompt: 'tanzen' is the same French word English borrowed after 1066 — give the English twin:
exercises.meaning: tanzen ↔ dance: one French word, two buyers
exercises.explanation: French danser went to both languages: English took it at court, German borrowed tanzen from the same neighbour. The aha is free — you already owned the word, dressed in English sounds.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the frequency sentence: 'I seldom dance'
exercises.explanation: selten lands right after the verb, like English seldom. oft and nie live in the same slot: Ich tanze oft, Ich tanze nie.
exercises.affirmation: Selten is not never — the sentence leaves the door open.

diagnosis.slip: reaching for ich tanzt — the -t ending
diagnosis.cue: ich takes the bare stem: ich tanze, du tanzt

exercises.prompt: Assemble the weekday sentence: 'On a weekday I have an appointment'
exercises.target_answer: Am Wochentag habe ich einen Termin
exercises.meaning: On a weekday I have an appointment

vocab_hints.note: am Wochentag — on the weekday; am is the contraction of an + dem.

exercises.explanation: der Termin — the appointment — lives on the Wochentag, the weekday; the weekend belongs to the hobbies. And Wochentag decomposes exactly like its English cousins: Woche is week, Tag is day.

summary.outcome: Name the hobbies — Musik, Sport, Lied, tanzen, malen — and say how often you do them.

use_example.german: Mein Hobby ist Musik — ich tanze selten, ich singe oft.
use_example.english: My hobby is music — I seldom dance, I often sing.

summary.takeaway: die Musik is the Muses' art, der Sport is English's own word sold back to German, das Lied's Old English twin leod is lost — and tanzen/dance are the same French purchase.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: when the hobbies throw a party — die Party, die Gitarre, reiten, das Schach, die Freizeit.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Hobbys I: die Musik, der Sport, das Lied, tanzen, malen (On a weekday I have an appointment):
twist.target_answer: Am Wochentag habe ich einen Termin
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Am Wochentag habe ich einen Termin" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Hobbys I: die Musik, der Sport, das Lied, tanzen, malen without relying on short-term echo.

musik.etymology_derivation: From Latin mūsica — the same Latin loan as English music. [wiktionary]

sport.etymology_derivation: 19th-century borrowing from English sport — see treiben (to drive) in Ich treibe Sport. [wiktionary]

lied.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *leuþ 'song'; no modern English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

tanzen.etymology_derivation: From Old French dancer via Low German — the same French loan as English dance. [wiktionary]

malen.etymology_derivation: From Mal 'spot, mark'; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

radio.context_translation: We listen to the radio in the car.
radio.etymology_derivation: Borrowed about 1920 from English radio, short for radiotelegraphy - a straight English loan. [wiktionary]

klavier.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French clavier, from Latin clavis 'key' — a Romance loan. [wiktionary]

hobby.etymology_derivation: An unadapted borrowing of English hobby — the same word, kept with German spelling and plural Hobbys. [wiktionary]

schuh.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *skōh — the true twin of English shoe (see Handschuh, hand-shoe). [wiktionary]

kino.context_translation: We are going to the cinema.
kino.etymology_derivation: Clipping of Kinematograph, the Greek-rooted invention name — a shared international loan. [wiktionary]

termin.context_phrase: Ich habe morgen einen Termin beim Zahnarzt.
termin.context_translation: I have a dentist appointment tomorrow.
termin.etymology_derivation: From Latin terminus, boundary or limit — the same Latin word that gives English term and terminus. [wiktionary]

wochentag.context_phrase: Am Wochentag arbeite ich bis fünf.
wochentag.context_translation: On a weekday I work until five.
wochentag.etymology_derivation: Woche + Tag — the exact compound of weekday; both elements are documented twins (week, day). [wiktionary]

selten.etymology_derivation: West Germanic *seldanā — the twin of English seldom, which the page lists as a cognate; German hardened d into t (seld- to selt-). [wiktionary]

verkäufer.context_phrase: Der Verkäufer zeigt mir die Schuhe.
verkäufer.context_translation: The salesman shows me the shoes.
verkäufer.etymology_derivation: Agent noun of verkaufen (sell, the kaufen/cheap family); English uses a different root for seller. [wiktionary]

bauer.context_phrase: Der Bauer wohnt auf dem Hof.
bauer.context_translation: The farmer lives on the farm.
bauer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *būraz "dweller" — cognate with English boor, and with bower "dwelling". [wiktionary]

türkei.context_phrase: Der Urlaub war in der Türkei.
türkei.etymology_derivation: Land of the Turks: from Medieval Latin Turcia, influenced by Türke "Turk". [wiktionary]

irland.etymology_derivation: The same name as English Ireland — land of the Irish, shared proper name. [wiktionary]

italienisch.etymology_derivation: Italien + the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; the same word as English Italian. [wiktionary]

arzt.context_translation: The doctor helps me a lot.
arzt.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German arzet, from Latin archīāter (chief healer); no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

rosa.etymology_derivation: Latin rosa loaned by both languages — English pink via French rose, same Latin source. [wiktionary]

sprache.context_phrase: Die Sprache ist schwer zu lernen.
sprache.context_translation: The language is hard to learn.
sprache.etymology_derivation: From Old High German sprāhha, Proto-West Germanic *sprāku, the twin of English speech; the k to ch velar shift links both to the sprechen and speak family. [wiktionary]

frühstück.context_phrase: Das Frühstück ist um sieben Uhr.
frühstück.etymology_derivation: Literally 'early piece (bite)': früh + Stück; NOT the break-fast calque English uses. [wiktionary]

socke.etymology_derivation: West Germanic borrowing from Latin soccus 'slipper' — a parallel borrowing with English sock. [wiktionary]

fahrrad.etymology_derivation: fahren (to drive, the fare root) + Rad (wheel): the driving-wheel. [wiktionary]

beruf.etymology_derivation: Literally the calling, deverbal of berufen (to call) - the same idea as English vocation (Latin vocare, to call), though the words are unrelated. [wiktionary]

feiertag.context_phrase: Heute ist ein Feiertag, alles ist zu.
feiertag.context_translation: Today is a public holiday, everything is closed.
feiertag.etymology_derivation: Feier + Tag — literally celebration day; Tag is the twin of day (d → t). [wiktionary]

sänger.etymology_derivation: Agent noun of singen (sing); initial s voices to [z] before vowels. [wiktionary]
